Semantic Works: HeadCam Studio: Episode 2: Dictate and Voice
October 2026

HeadCam Studio:
Episode 2: Dictate and Voice

Two ways to talk to an AI, and when to use each. Pasha asks ChatGPT the same question twice, once by dictation and once in a spoken conversation, and shows how he combines the two to get his work done without typing.

Dr. Pavel (Pasha) Simakov Managing Partner, Semantic Works LLC linkedin.com/in/pavelsimakov

00:00 – 00:27 · The use case

One question, asked two ways

Pasha paints in acrylic. One of his paintings exists as a gigapixel image, with an animation that flies through it at microscopic detail.

The question for this episode: how would he design that fly-through app with ChatGPT if he were starting today? He asks it twice:

  • Once by dictate: he talks, ChatGPT turns his speech into text, and answers in writing.
  • Once by voice: a spoken conversation, back and forth.

The question is the same. The conversations are not.

00:27 – 03:03 · Dictate

Dictate: say everything at once, get everything back

  • How Pasha uses it: he narrates every thought he has, in any order, for up to five minutes, then lets it run.
  • What he said: a gigapixel image; a smooth fly-through; browser or native Swift; SVG or WebGL; no third-party code; fast and buttery smooth.
  • What came back: an excellent answer, untangled from the jumble: tiling, smoothness, canvas versus Swift, and a choice of WebGL 2.0.
  • The cost: a lot said in, a lot to read out. Expect to spend time going through the answer.
I said a lot, in no particular order … Even though I spoke out of order about many different things, it did an excellent job.Pasha
03:03 – 08:46 · Voice

Voice: a conversation that has to get to the point

Because it answers aloud, ChatGPT cannot read out five pages. It has to pick what matters most for the very next reply, so the conversation stays at the top level and moves fast:

  • Tiling first: never load the whole image; cut it into a pyramid of zoom levels.
  • No WebGL needed, and SVG is for vector graphics, not huge bitmaps.
  • A turn in seconds: it suggested OpenSeadragon; Pasha said no third-party code; it answered with plain JavaScript, canvas 2D and tiles made offline.
  • When to go native: aim for 60 frames per second; consider Swift only below 30.

One catch, as of October 2026: unless interrupted, the voice keeps talking.

The difference

Dictate or voice? It depends on the moment

DictateVoice
You giveEverything on your mind, up to five minutes, in any orderA sentence or two at a time
You getA thorough, written answer that covers it allThe single most relevant point, spoken
PaceSlow: time to read the answerFast: you steer and interrupt
Best forSpecifying, designing, reviewingExploring options and choosing a direction
Watch out forA lot to readIt keeps talking unless you interrupt
08:46 – 10:01 · How Pasha combines them

Explore by voice, then specify and review by dictate

  • 1. Explore by voice. Talk through the options quickly, without going deep, and choose a direction.
  • 2. Specify by dictate. Narrate the use cases, like a product requirements document or a system architecture.
  • 3. Review by dictate. Read a document and say what you think as you go ("paragraph one is good; page two needs a new opening"), then ask for a summary of the notes. The same works for an app: use it, and narrate how it feels and where the rough corners are.
I start with voice and explore the space. Once I've chosen a direction, I switch to dictate …Pasha
10:01 – 10:30 · Why no typing

No keyboard, by choice

Pasha first stopped typing because of a pinched nerve, and typing hurt. The nerve has healed, but he never went back.

Everything he does with AI now runs on two buttons: voice to explore, dictate to specify and review.
